core: the working definition of cost of capital: the return that providers of money require for letting a business use their funds (CFI: the minimum rate of return a business must earn before generating value; OpenStax: what providers of capital expect in return)
cost of debt (interest on borrowing) and cost of equity (the return owners expect) each stated in one line
the core rule: a project must earn more than the cost of the money funding it, with an original example
the weighted idea: the overall cost of capital is a blend of all funding sources, each weighted by its share of the total (no WACC formula depth)
cost of capital as a hurdle rate: the minimum return a project must clear before it is accepted
risk and the cost: riskier businesses face higher required returns from providers of money
the honest framing: the cost of capital is the business's floor for ambition
supporting: the cost of debt as the interest rate a company would pay to refinance its existing debt
the cost of equity cannot be observed directly in the market and must be estimated
the weights of all funding sources sum to 100% of a company's financing
the weighted average cost of capital is an estimate resting on assumptions, not a precise figure
higher default risk raises the cost of new debt and also pushes up the return shareholders expect

claims.claim: CFI defines the cost of capital as the minimum rate of return that a business must earn before generating value; before a business can turn a profit, it must at least generate sufficient income to cover the cost of the capital it uses to fund its operations.

OpenStax Principles of Finance frames the cost of capital from the providers' side: the costs of debt and equity capital are what company lenders (those who allow the firm to use their capital) expect in return for providing that capital.

The cost of debt is the interest rate a company pays on its existing debt (CFI), which OpenStax specifies as the interest rate it would have to pay to refinance its existing debt; the cost of equity is the expected return on the shareholders' investment (CFI), which OpenStax notes cannot be directly observed in the market and must be estimated.

A project the company invests in must be equal to or ideally greater than its cost of capital (CFI); the cost of capital is used as the discount rate for the company's free cash flows in DCF analysis (CFI).

The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is the most common approach to calculating a company's cost of capital: all sources of financing are included, and each source is weighted relative to its proportion in the company's capital structure (CFI); OpenStax adds that the weights of all sources must sum to 100% because the company must account for all of its financing.

A hurdle rate is the minimum required or target rate of return that investors expect to receive on an investment; before accepting an investment project, its expected return must be equal to or greater than the hurdle rate, and most companies use their weighted average cost of capital (WACC) as the hurdle rate for investments.

Risk raises the cost of capital: for a company with a lot of debt, adding new debt increases its risk of default, and a higher default risk increases the cost of debt as new lenders demand a premium; shareholders also expect a premium over the return on debt for taking on additional risk (CFI). OpenStax agrees that changes in the overall riskiness of the firm change the price of the debt securities it has issued.

The WACC that financial managers derive depends on the assumptions and models they use for weights and capital costs; it is an estimate based on assumptions such as the risk-free interest rate, the market risk premium, and a firm's beta (OpenStax).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame the cost of capital from opposite sides of the same exchange: CFI emphasizes the business's side (the minimum rate of return a business must earn before generating value), while OpenStax emphasizes the providers' side (what lenders and owners expect in return for providing capital).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the two framings as complementary and attributes each to its source: the return providers require IS the return the business must earn. The working definition combines them — 'the return that providers of money require for letting a business use their funds' — with both attributions present.

conflictingEvidence.issue: OpenStax notes that different estimation methods for the cost of equity (CAPM versus constant dividend growth model) produce different values, so no single precise cost of capital exists.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the weighted average cost of capital as an estimate resting on assumptions, avoiding any suggestion of a single precise figure.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; aiIngestionAllowed:false per subject source-map). openstax.org blocks direct fetch; read via an Internet Archive capture (2022-09-30) on 2026-08-21 and restated. Supports: the costs of debt and equity capital as what company lenders (those who allow the firm to use their capital) expect in return for providing that capital; a company's cost of debt as the interest rate it would have to pay to refinance its existing debt; the cost of common stock capital as not directly observable in the market and therefore estimated; changes in the overall riskiness of the firm changing the price of its debt securities; the after-tax cost of debt and the tax deductibility of interest (noted, not taught in depth).

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; aiIngestionAllowed:false per subject source-map). Read via an Internet Archive capture (2022-09-29) on 2026-08-21 and restated. Supports: WACC as calculated once the weights in a company's capital structure and the costs of the different sources are known; the weights of debt, preferred stock, and common equity summing to 100% of the company's financing; the WACC as an estimate based on assumptions (risk-free rate, market risk premium, beta) rather than a precise figure. Formula depth intentionally not taught (lesson literacy level).

Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
